about: CloudBridge Summit 2026 is a fictional demo event, generated from CLOUDBRIDGE-SKETCH.md on Nov 9 2026. Every person, company and room in this file is invented, and the UI labels the event as fictional. Session times are venue-local wall-clock times in the conference time zone; the loader stores them as UTC instants (TIME-1). Persona preferences are private, explicit choices (PRIV-1).

sessions.title: Bridges, Not Silos: Running Clusters With AI Teammates (opening keynote)
sessions.abstract: The opening keynote. Larkspur Logistics runs its clusters with an AI SRE agent as a teammate: it triages alerts, gathers evidence and drafts fixes, while people decide what merges. Maya Okafor shares what changed for the on-call rotation, where the agent saves hours, and why every bridge between humans and agents needs a review step.

sessions.title: AI SRE in Practice: What Our Agent Got Wrong
sessions.abstract: Our AI SRE agent once blamed a healthy database for an outage, with total confidence, and it was wrong. This talk replays the incident step by step: the evidence the agent saw, the evidence it ignored, and the guardrail that stopped its fix before it reached production. You will leave with a checklist for agent-assisted incident response: demand evidence links, keep every change reviewable, and make it cheap for a human to say no.

sessions.title: OpenTelemetry From Zero to Traces in One Afternoon
sessions.abstract: New to observability? This beginner session instruments a small web service with OpenTelemetry from scratch: traces first, then metrics and logs that share the same trace ID. We set up a collector, keep the sampling defaults simple, and show three questions traces answer that logs alone cannot. No tracing experience needed.

sessions.title: Golden Paths That People Actually Walk
sessions.abstract: A golden path only helps if developers choose to walk it. Kenji Moriyama shares how Brightpath Cloud's platform team rebuilt its service templates around developer interviews, measured adoption, and retired the paths nobody used. Learn to run your internal developer platform as a product, with defaults, docs and feedback loops that keep it walkable.

sessions.title: Kernel Eyes: Watching Every Syscall Without Slowing Down
sessions.abstract: eBPF lets you watch every syscall, file open and network connection on a node without changing a single application. Hannah Ostrowski shows how Quillon Labs built runtime security detection on eBPF probes that stays under one percent CPU overhead, and which kernel events are worth that cost. We also cover tuning noisy rules, rolling out new detections safely, and what eBPF still cannot see.

sessions.title: GitOps Rollbacks Under Pressure
sessions.abstract: When a bad deploy hits production at 2 a.m., how fast can you roll back? Marcus Bell runs rollback drills with a GitOps controller: reverting the commit, handling database migrations that cannot be undone, and keeping clusters in sync while the incident is still open. Leave with a rollback runbook you can test this week.

sessions.title: Cost Signals for Kubernetes Teams
sessions.abstract: Cloud bills arrive a month late, far too late to change a team's habits. Leila Haddad shows how Larkspur Logistics turned Kubernetes resource requests, idle capacity and per-namespace costs into daily signals that teams actually read. Learn which FinOps metrics led to real savings, and which only started arguments.

sessions.title: Accessible Dashboards for On-Call Humans
sessions.abstract: At 3 a.m. an on-call engineer may be tired, color-blind, zoomed to 200 percent or using a screen reader. This beginner-friendly observability session shows how to design dashboards and alerts everyone can read: palettes with enough contrast, charts with text alternatives, and alert messages that say what to do next. No design background needed.

sessions.title: Operating Kubernetes Agents Safely
sessions.abstract: An AI agent with cluster-admin rights can break production faster than any human. This advanced session covers keeping Kubernetes agents safe: least-privilege service accounts, dry runs and approval gates, blast-radius limits, and audit trails you can replay. Daniel Kowalczyk shares the guardrails Quillon Labs added after its agents began acting on their own diagnoses.

sessions.title: Search That Understands Your Docs: Hybrid Retrieval for Internal Portals
sessions.abstract: Keyword search finds the exact error code; semantic search finds the page that explains the idea in different words. Ananya Iyer shows why combining both, BM25 and vector search in Elasticsearch fused with reciprocal rank fusion, beats either one alone on a real internal developer portal. We cover chunking, evaluating with golden queries, and telling when hybrid retrieval is worth its cost.

sessions.title: Sampling Without Regret
sessions.abstract: For teams already running OpenTelemetry at scale, keeping every trace gets expensive fast. This advanced session compares head and tail sampling in the collector, shows how Tidewater Health keeps every error and slow trace while dropping most routine ones, and explains how to keep metrics accurate after sampling. Expect real collector configurations and the trade-offs behind them.

sessions.title: Fleet Upgrades Without Weekends
sessions.abstract: Larkspur Logistics upgrades more than forty Kubernetes clusters every quarter, and nobody gives up a weekend for it anymore. Tomasz Nowicki explains the upgrade pipeline: canary clusters, automated checks for deprecated APIs, node pool surges, and a rollback plan for every step. Learn to make version upgrades routine operations instead of heroic projects.

sessions.title: Policy as Code for Humans
sessions.abstract: Admission policies keep insecure workloads out of your clusters, but only if developers understand why a deploy was rejected. Fatima Al-Sayed shows how Brightpath Cloud writes policy as code with clear messages, tests policies like any other code, and rolls out new rules in audit mode first. Good error messages turned security policy from a blocker into a guide.

sessions.title: Your First Operator
sessions.abstract: Operators extend Kubernetes with your own resources and controllers. In this beginner session Chris Adeyemi builds a small operator live, from a custom resource definition to a reconcile loop that repairs drift. You will learn when an operator is the right tool, and when a plain Deployment and a script are enough.

sessions.title: Load Shedding: Saying No Gracefully
sessions.abstract: When traffic exceeds capacity, an overloaded service that tries to answer everyone ends up answering no one. Maya Okafor covers load shedding and admission control in practice: rejecting early with a clear 503 and Retry-After, protecting the requests that matter most, and autoscaling that catches up instead of thrashing. Includes the dashboards and alerts that show shedding is working.

sessions.title: Inclusive Incident Reviews
sessions.abstract: Blameless incident reviews can still leave people out: those who missed the call, those who rely on captions, and those new to the team. Owen Brightwater shares a review format that works for everyone, with a written timeline shared before the meeting, captioned recordings, and room for quieter voices. Accessible reviews produce better fixes.

sessions.title: Autonomous Cluster Security: Promises and Limits
sessions.abstract: Some vendors promise AI agents that detect and stop attacks on their own. Hannah Ostrowski tests that promise with an autonomous agent acting on eBPF runtime signals, measured against simulated attacks and real false positives. See where it helps, how it can break production by quarantining the wrong workload, and the human checkpoints that keep it honest.

sessions.title: Tracing LLM Calls in Production
sessions.abstract: Large language model calls are slow, expensive and nondeterministic, so they need tracing more than most dependencies. Ananya Iyer traces LLM calls with OpenTelemetry: spans for latency and token cost, metrics for spend per feature, and the things you should never log, such as prompts that carry user data. Learn to explain a slow or costly answer without leaking anything private.

sessions.title: Platform APIs Your Developers Will Love
sessions.abstract: Every internal platform is an API, whether anyone designed it or not. Kenji Moriyama covers platform APIs with clear contracts, versioning and self-service, so developers get what they need without filing tickets. Includes lessons from Brightpath Cloud's move from ticket queues to a declarative platform API.

sessions.title: AI Foundations for Platform Teams
sessions.abstract: A plain-language introduction to the AI vocabulary platform teams hear every day: models, tokens, embeddings, retrieval and evaluation. Marcus Bell explains each idea with small examples, what it costs to run, and the questions to ask before adopting an AI feature. Made for beginners; no machine learning background needed.

sessions.title: Chaos Days Without Chaos
sessions.abstract: Chaos engineering finds weaknesses before your customers do, as long as the experiment itself is safe. Tomasz Nowicki shares how Larkspur Logistics runs quarterly chaos days: a clear hypothesis, a limited blast radius, automatic aborts, and findings that become reliability work. Includes the experiment templates the team reuses.

sessions.title: Secrets Management at Scale
sessions.abstract: Secrets sprawl across clusters, pipelines and laptops faster than anyone can rotate them. Fatima Al-Sayed covers secrets management at scale on Kubernetes: external secret stores, short-lived credentials through workload identity, automatic rotation, and catching leaked keys before attackers do. See how Brightpath Cloud removed long-lived credentials from its CI pipelines.

sessions.title: From Alert to Pull Request: Automating the Last Mile
sessions.abstract: An alert fires, an agent investigates, and minutes later a pull request proposes the fix, often a rollback of the bad deploy or a resource change. Leila Haddad walks through automating that last mile with GitOps: how the agent gathers evidence, why the fix is always a reviewed pull request, and how the pipeline verifies recovery after the merge. Includes the cases where automation should stop and page a human.

sessions.title: What We Learned Building With Agents (closing panel)
sessions.abstract: The closing panel. Daniel Kowalczyk, Hannah Ostrowski and Chris Adeyemi look back on three days of talks on AI SRE, security and Kubernetes, and debate what agents should and should not do in cluster operations. Bring your questions for the panel.

cues.text: Let me show you the morning our AI SRE agent got it wrong.
At six twelve, the checkout latency alarm fired.
Within forty seconds the agent had a diagnosis: the primary database was saturated,
and it proposed a failover. It wrote a confident summary, with graphs.
The database was fine.
What the agent had seen was a jump in connection errors.
What it had ignored was a config push nine minutes earlier
that set the connection pool to zero on three of our twelve pods.
The failover would have cost us about nine minutes of write downtime, for nothing.
The guardrail that caught it was boring, and that is the point.
Every change the agent proposes becomes a pull request with evidence links,
and a human has to approve it.
Our on-call engineer opened the first link, saw that the errors came from three pods only,
and rejected the fix in one click.
So here is my checklist.
Demand evidence links, not summaries. Keep every change reviewable.
And make it cheap for a human to say no.
Our internal developer portal had a search box that everyone ignored. Here is why.
Keyword search was great when you knew the exact words.
Type the error code E4031 and the runbook came up first.
But ask why does my deploy hang after the health check, and you got nothing,
because the runbook says readiness probe timeout.
Semantic search was the mirror image. It understood the question,
but it would rank a general page about probes above the one runbook that mentioned E4031.
So we stopped choosing. We run both queries in Elasticsearch:
BM25 for the words, and a k-nearest-neighbors query over embeddings for the meaning,
with the same filters on both.
Then we fuse the two ranked lists with reciprocal rank fusion.
Each document scores one over sixty plus its rank in each list, and the sums decide the order.
No tuning, no learned weights.
On our forty golden queries, the right page landed in the top five
sixty-one percent of the time with keywords alone, and eighty-four percent with the hybrid.
The cost is two queries instead of one, and that was worth it.
A language model call is the slowest, most expensive and least predictable dependency
most of us have ever added to a request path. So trace it like one.
Every call in our service gets its own span.
We record the model name, the input and output token counts, an estimated cost,
and whether the response was served from cache. The latency is the span itself.
What we never record is the prompt.
The prompt carries the user's own words, and a trace is not a safe place for them.
We also keep the model's answer out of the span attributes.
If we need to debug the content, we do it with a sampled, access-controlled store, not with telemetry.
With that in place, a slow answer stops being a mystery.
Last month one feature doubled its p95 latency.
The spans showed retries: every timeout was being retried twice,
so one slow model call turned into three.
We also roll the token counts into a metric: cost per feature, per hour.
The first week it ran, it found an internal tool that spent more than the product did.
